notes.meaning: The boundary line for the descendants of Joseph started at the Jordan River near Jericho and climbed westward through the desert into the hills around Bethel. Joseph received a double share of the land because the birthright of the firstborn son passed to his family. God directed the lot to grant these brother tribes a fertile homeland right in the center of Canaan.

The boundary went on from Bethel toward the town of Luz and continued to the region of the Archites near Ataroth. Bethel and Luz were once separate neighboring places that gradually came to be known together. God outlined the path clearly so the families knew exactly where their district began.

From there, the border descended westward past the land of the Japhletites toward Lower Beth-horon and Gezer, ending at the Mediterranean Sea. Beth-horon guarded an important mountain roadway, and Gezer was a prominent fortress down near the coastal plain. God laid out these natural markers to establish the full westward reach of the tribe.

The half-tribe of Manasseh and the tribe of Ephraim, the two sons of Joseph, received this tract as their inheritance. They settled their lands early along with Judah so they could protect the rest of Israel at the main camp. God fulfilled his promise to their forefather Joseph by giving his sons a prominent place in the land.

The record turns to the specific borders given to the clans of Ephraim, running from Ataroth-addar over to Upper Beth-horon. Upper Beth-horon sat on a ridge just above the lower town, watching over the steep mountain pass. Although these ancient border descriptions can seem difficult to trace today, they gave each family a secure and definite home.

Ephraim's line stretched toward the Mediterranean Sea on the west, while on the north it curved east past Michmethath to Taanath-shiloh and Janoah. Taanath-shiloh was an eastern town distinct from the main sanctuary town of Shiloh. God carefully marked out these turns and towns to set peaceful limits between neighboring tribes.

From Janoah the border sloped downward toward Ataroth and Naarah, reaching the district of Jericho before finishing at the Jordan River. This border reached the territory surrounding Jericho rather than the city itself, which was later assigned to Benjamin. God gave Ephraim clear water and mountain boundaries to safeguard their inheritance.

On the northwest, the boundary ran from Tappuah along the Brook of Kanah until it reached the Mediterranean Sea. Tappuah stood on the border shared with Manasseh, and the valley of Kanah formed a natural divide between them. God defined each border marker so both tribes could live together in order and clarity.

Ephraim was also granted extra cities and nearby villages situated inside the borders of Manasseh. Because Ephraim had a larger population than the western half of Manasseh, additional territory was shared with them. This shared inheritance met Ephraim's practical needs and encouraged the brother tribes to support one another.

Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanite people living in Gezer, but instead allowed them to stay as forced laborers. This compromise violated God's clear instruction to remove the idolatrous inhabitants completely. Relying on tribute and forced labor instead of total obedience led to serious spiritual harm for Israel in later years.

other.view: Some modern scholars suggest that the phrase 'to this day' points to a later editor who added historical details long after the original events took place.
